Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
1252 PM EST Wed Nov 4 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 223 AM EST Wednesday...

Today's high temperatures were slightly increased.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 223 AM EST Wednesday...

1. Near record high temperatures are expected today with mostly
sunny conditions and limited, localized fire weather concerns.

2. Showers are expected on Thursday and possibly linger into 
Thursday night, then mainly dry weather will follow for Friday. 
No impactful weather is expected.

3. Periodic showers are possible over the weekend into early 
next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 223 AM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Record high temperatures for the date remain on 
track for today; see Climate section of the forecast discussion 
for details. Progged 925 millibar temperatures of 16 to 18 
Celsius, near climatological maximum values, supports high 
temperatures in the low to mid 70s with dry adiabatic lapse 
rates across our valley locations. The most unusually extreme 
temperatures are favored for the Adirondacks and northeastern 
Vermont, where the Extreme Forecast Index most recent run shows 
a high confidence of near record high temperatures. This has 
trended more extreme with time, so we have used the 90th 
percentile temperature guidance for high temperatures. The 
resulting forecast highs look consistent with recent 
verification of observed temperatures and for a scenario with 
sunshine and warm air advection from the southwest. Relative 
humidity will remain fairly moderate based on guidance and 
observed values upstream in the Midwest, putting a likely 
minimum in the 40% range. A few wind gusts may exceed 25 MPH 
this morning with channeled flow in the Champlain Valley, but 
winds aloft generally look too light to cause much concern even 
if boundary layer mixing is deeper than modeled.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A weakening cold front will put an end to our 
dry and very warm weather. Two rounds of showers appears on the 
docket for Thursday, with the first round being relatively 
disordered showers tied to a surge of anomalous moisture sliding
northeastward through our region. This precipitation looks 
strongly forced with relatively deep moisture such that rain 
chances will be nearly certain for at least a brief period of 
time during the daytime hours. Towards evening, while moisture 
will be more limited, sufficiently steep lapse rates to yield a 
ribbon of instability and a chance of loosely organized showers 
that will track to the east across northern Vermont Thursday 
night. As the front exits/washes out to our east, think flow 
will be light enough amidst rich near surface moisture to 
support some patchy fog and drizzle regardless of how widespread
these evening showers wind up being. The lack of a wind shift 
will keep temperatures and humidity above normal into Friday. 
However, conditions look mainly dry with our region sitting 
between an inverted trough to our east and an incoming upper 
level low to our west. Most likely rainfall amounts being 
offered are mainly 0.1" to 0.33", but with convective nature of 
some of the rain, footprints will be quite variable.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Upper level troughing will likely settle over 
eastern Canada and the Northeast as the longwave pattern is 
favored to stall Saturday through the weekend. Model consensus 
points to multiple rounds of rainfall associated with upper 
level low overhead and potential for surface low pressure to 
gyre and pivot back westward early next week while a series of 
troughs move through the base of the longwave overhead. The 
result will be for more shower chances Saturday onward with 
temperatures cooling back into the 50s and upper 40s. Elevation 
dependent snowfall could occur with the cold pool expected to be
over the region. It's feasible that there could be some lower 
elevation pellet showers should the troughs be more energetic as
they move through. This pattern will favor cooler overnight 
lows as well with lower elevations in the 30s and mid/upper 20s 
above 1500-2000ft through Monday. There are some indications 
that reinforcing cold air may occur by Tuesday possibly pushing 
temperatures lower Tuesday night.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 18Z Thursday...Conditions will primarily be VFR at all
sites. Southerly breezes are expected to be around 10 mph with 
some gusts 15 to 20 kts at times. Highest gusts will be at PBG 
and MSS where flow is more channeled and could top out around 25
kts. Winds decrease after 20Z with clouds increasing and 
lowering overnight. Showers will begin moving into the St 
Lawrence Valley after 06Z as a front approaches. Have included
6SM -SHRA as rain spreads southwest to northeast across our 
area between 12-18z.


Outlook...

Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Patchy BR.
Friday: VFR. Slight chance RA.
Friday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance RA.
Saturday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Chance RA.
Saturday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas IFR possible. Chance RA.
Sunday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Slight chance RA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Slight chance
RA.
Monday: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Chance RA.

&&
